activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
The studio smelled of resin and old radiator heat, and Mrs. Okoye's metronome sat on the piano lid like a small brass beetle that had wandered in from another century, anachronistic now that everyone kept time on their phones. Rachel unwrapped her cello on the second Tuesday of September, the same way she had every Tuesday for six years, and set the music on the stand: the Chopin polonaise she had taught herself over the summer, the piece she could play from memory with her eyes closed.

She got through the opening page before Mrs. Okoye raised one hand. Not the palm-out gesture of a conductor, just two fingers lifted off her knee, the way you would signal a waiter for the check.

"Play measures forty-one and forty-two," Mrs. Okoye said.

"They're awful," Rachel said. "That's why I skipped to the part I know."

"That's why we're playing them."

Rachel set her bow back on the string. The two bars contained a shift from third position to a harmonic she could not reliably find, followed by a string crossing her left hand wanted no part of. She missed the harmonic. She missed it again. On the fourth attempt she got it and then fumbled the crossing immediately after, which felt somehow worse, because it proved the problem was not one problem but two.

"Again," Mrs. Okoye said, and turned the metronome to sixty. "Just the shift. Nothing after it."

They spent the rest of the half hour on those two bars and a stretch in the slow movement that Rachel had been papering over since June. When the lesson ended, Mrs. Okoye wrote the measure numbers on a sticky note and pressed it to the inside of Rachel's folder like a prescription. "The polonaise can wait," she said. "It will still be there."

At home, Rachel did what she always did after a hard lesson: she played the polonaise from the top, the whole glorious run of it, fast enough that the hard passages blurred past on momentum. It felt wonderful. It felt like the summer itself, all that freedom she'd had before senior year started grinding. And then she recorded herself on her phone, because Mrs. Okoye had asked her to once, and listened back, and heard the truth. The shift was still a hole in the recording, a small swallowed silence exactly where the harmonic should have been. Playing the piece through had not fixed it. Playing the piece through had mostly let her practice not noticing.

That night she found the book. Her brother had left a stack of them in the garage when he moved out, and one was about how people get good at things. She read a chapter before bed, sitting on her floor with her back against the bed frame. The chapter had a phrase in it, deliberate practice, which it defined as working on specific weaknesses with a clear goal and immediate feedback, and it claimed this improved skill more than simply playing through pieces already known. She read the sentence twice. Then she thought about the sticky note in her folder, and the hole in the recording, and the fact that Mrs. Okoye had never once let her play a piece straight through in a lesson, and she understood that this was not cruelty or habit. It was policy. Her teacher had been running the experiment for six years and Rachel had only now read the results.

The next morning she tried it. She set her phone to record, picked a single goal, land the harmonic cleanly four times in a row, and played only the shift, nothing else, twenty times. Each time she listened back immediately. The misses sounded different once she could hear them: some were late fingers, some were a crooked thumb under the neck. She fixed one thing at a time. It was the least fun hour of cello she had ever spent, and at the end of it the harmonic was still not perfect, but it was honest. She could hear exactly how far off she was, which meant she knew exactly what to do Tuesday.

She kept at it for a week. On Thursday her friend Dana came over and asked why Rachel was playing the same three seconds of music over and over like a scratched CD, and Rachel tried to explain. Dana watched her miss the harmonic six consecutive times and said, "This looks miserable. Why not just play the fun part?"

"Because the fun part doesn't change anything," Rachel said. Dana shrugged and went to raid the kitchen, and Rachel went back to the shift, and she noticed she did not entirely disagree with Dana either. There was something in the repetition that closed the world down to a pinhole, and she missed the wide way the polonaise used to open up under her hands. She had not abrogated her right to enjoy it, she decided; she had only set it aside for a season, like a coat in summer.

There was also her mother to negotiate, because on Saturday her mother heard the same three seconds eleven times through the living room wall and came to the doorway with dish towel in hand. They reached a detente of sorts: Rachel would drill before noon, and after dinner she could play whatever she wanted, as loud as she wanted, and her mother would not say a word about the conservatory application sitting unfinished on the kitchen table.

Tuesday came. In the studio, Mrs. Okoye did not ask for the polonaise. She asked for measure forty-one, and Rachel set her bow and placed the shift, and the harmonic bloomed out clean and round, and then the crossing, which she had practiced separately all week, followed it like a sentence that had finally found its verb. She played the two bars again to be sure. The second time was clean too, though a little careful, and the third time, when Mrs. Okoye nodded once and turned the metronome up to sixty-six, was clean and not careful at all.

"Interesting week," Mrs. Okoye said, tapping the sticky note. "You found something."

"I read my brother's book," Rachel said. "It called it deliberate practice. Working on the specific weakness, with a goal, and feedback right away. Better than playing what you already know." She looked down at the strings. "The part I can't decide is whether I like it. It works. I just don't know if I want to like something that works."

Mrs. Okoye considered that for a moment, then set a new piece on the stand, a sonata Rachel had never seen, and pointed to the third line, where the notes clustered thick and low near the frog of the bow.

"We'll start there," she said. "Measure forty's all yours."

story:
The keys were colder than Jordan expected, as though the car had been waiting in the driveway overnight with its own opinion about being driven. His father stood by the mailbox with his coffee, but it was Ms. Aroyo, the instructor, who held the clipboard, a saturnine woman of about sixty who had apparently decided that encouragement was a resource to be rationed.

"Seatbelt," she said. "Mirrors. Tell me what you see."

Jordan adjusted the mirror until the driveway's hedge filled it, then corrected until the road appeared, empty and gray at seven in the morning. He had waited two years for this, through a knee surgery that had emptied his savings and a winter of riding the bus past the hospital where his grandmother was slowly forgetting things. She had offered her old sedan for the lesson, and it sat in the driveway now with a rosary still looped around the rearview mirror, which Ms. Aroyo had looked at and, to her credit, not touched.

"Signal, check over your shoulder, and pull out when it's clear," she said. He did it, the car lurching once before he found the friction point, and then they were on the road, doing twenty-five in a quiet neighborhood, his hands at ten and two like the manual had shown. His father shrank in the mirror to a small waving figure by the mailbox and then was gone.

At the second stop sign, Ms. Aroyo asked him to pull over. "A question," she said. "You're going twenty. Now imagine you're going forty, twice as fast. How much longer does the car need to stop? Guess."

"Twice," Jordan said. She waited. He thought of his physics teacher, Mr. Okafor, who had once drawn a curve on the board and called the class's intuition lazy. "No, wait. It's the square. Braking distance is proportional to the square of your speed, so doubling the speed makes the braking distance about four times as long." He said it and then heard himself say it, the way you sometimes only understand a thing aloud.

"Right," Ms. Aroyo said, and there was, briefly, something almost warm in it. "So what does that mean for how you drive?"

"It means the road lies to you," Jordan said. "Twenty feels safe and forty feels kind of safe and they're not the same at all. You get desensitized. Like people who drive this street every day and roll the stop signs because nothing has ever happened here."

She made a mark on her clipboard. "Keep going."

He drove on, and the neighborhood opened onto a wider road, and Jordan found himself thinking about his grandmother, who had taught his mother to drive in a church parking lot and who now, when he visited, argued calmly that the thermostat and the bank and the traffic lights were all run by the same unelected technocracy, a word she had picked up from television and wielded at nurses. He had always corrected her, gently, and she had always smiled at him in a way that suggested she found his corrections decorative. Two ways of seeing the world, hers and his, and lately he had begun to suspect that neither one was complete. She distrusted everything she couldn't see working; he trusted systems so completely that he had never once wondered what a car was doing when he pressed the brake.

Ahead, a ball rolled out from between two parked cars, followed a half second later by a small dog, no child behind it, but Jordan braked hard anyway, the seatbelt biting his shoulder, the car stopping well short, and his heart going like a clock in another room.

"Good," Ms. Aroyo said. "You saw the ball and read the whole sentence, not just the first word." She let the silence sit for a moment. "Now, at twice this speed, could you have stopped in that space?"

He looked at the distance between the bumper and the ball, still rocking gently in the gutter. Four times as long, he thought. He tried to picture it stretching down the block, past the hedges, past the house with the flag, and he found he couldn't be sure his own foot would have been fast enough even in the space he'd had. That, at least, he was willing to admit he didn't know.

"No," he said. "I don't think so."

"Correct answer is 'no,'" she said. "The honest one, anyway."

They drove back with the windows cracked, the rosary swinging gently at every turn. When they pulled into the driveway, his father was still out by the mailbox, coffee gone cold in his hands, pretending he hadn't been standing there the whole time. Jordan put the car in park and looked at the rosary a moment, then reached up and turned it so the beads hung straight.

"Same time next week?" Ms. Aroyo asked.

"Same time," Jordan said, and shook her hand through the window, and behind him, the engine ticked as it cooled.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
story:
The workbook had come from the library in town, four days overdue, and Joshua read it in the hayloft because that was the only place on the farm where nobody asked him for anything. In ten days he was supposed to be at the university, sitting in a lecture hall for the first time in his life, and the orientation packet had included a page of review material with the words "transcription and translation" underlined twice, as though everyone in the world already knew what they meant. He did not. He read about a strand of DNA being copied into a message, and the message being read out to build a protein, and he copied the diagrams onto the back of a feed receipt until the ladder shapes looked like the fence rows he'd walked since he was six.

The chart was what stopped him. It listed the four letters of the code, A and T and G and C, and it said the letters were read in groups of three, called codons. He did the arithmetic himself on the receipt, multiplying it out in the margin: four choices for the first position, four for the second, four for the third. Sixty-four possible codons. Then he counted the names along the side of the chart, the amino acids, the building blocks the codons stood for. He counted twice, touching each one with the pencil. Twenty.

He was sure he had it wrong, the way he'd been sure, the first time he rebuilt an irrigation pump, that the gasket went on the outside. He went down the rows of the chart letter by letter. Leucine appeared again and again, under codon after codon. Serine the same. Six of the sixty-four all pointed at the same amino acid, and he sat back against the bales with the receipt in his lap and the dust moving in the light, and he thought that the code was wasteful, or that it was generous, and he could not yet tell which. He had always tried to dichotomize things into broken or working, but the chart refused the sorting. "There are sixty-four codons," he said out loud to the empty loft, "and only twenty amino acids. Most of them have more than one codon." Saying it made it real, the way saying a prayer did, though he hadn't prayed since the funeral.

His grandfather would have understood it in a minute. Eli Ozawa had saved seed his whole life, forty years of choosing which wheat to plant and which to let go, and he had died in March without ever hearing the word codon. It was Eli who had paid the deposit on the university, out of an ascetic savings account that held almost nothing else, and Joshua had promised him at the hospital bed that he would learn the science of it, the part Eli had done by instinct and by hand. The promise had felt clean then. Now it felt like the apportionment of an estate, everybody getting a share of a man who could not be divided.

His sister Ruth found him at the kitchen table that evening with the chart propped against the salt shaker. She was fifteen and had already announced she was not leaving, that the farm needed somebody with both hands and no lectures to attend. "Read it to me," she said, not sitting, holding a pail of eggs she refused to set down, and he understood she was not asking about biology.

"You take the DNA and you copy a stretch of it into a message," he said. "That's transcription. Then the message gets read in threes, each three standing for one amino acid, and the amino acids get strung into a protein. That's translation. But here's the thing." He turned the chart toward her. "Sixty-four threes are possible. Twenty building blocks. Lots of threes mean the same thing."

Ruth set the pail down finally. She looked at the chart the way she looked at a sick heifer, steadily, looking for the lie in it. "So there's more ways to say a thing than there are things to say."

"That's one way to put it."

She was quiet while the kettle ticked. From where Ruth stood, the whole scene looked different than it had from the loft: her brother hunched over the table like their grandfather over seed trays, and on the wall behind him the map of the university town, already creased from handling. She had spent a month being angry at him for going, dividing the family neatly into the one who stayed and the one who left, and the chart had just broken the arithmetic. He could go and still be of this place. The words were many; the meaning was one. She hated that it comforted her, and it comforted her anyway.

"Grandpa never knew this," Joshua said. "Forty years and he never knew why the wheat worked." He looked at the chart again, at the rows of threes, at the twenty names, and he knew he would explain it in a lecture hall someday and get part of it wrong and be corrected in front of two hundred strangers, and he knew he would not be able to ask Eli whether the deposit had been worth it. "I can't decide if it's sloppy or if it's the whole point."

Ruth picked up the pail and carried it toward the cellar door. At the threshold she turned. "Say the codon thing again, the numbers. I want to get it right for Dad."

"Sixty-four and twenty," Joshua said. "Most have more than one." She nodded once and went down the stairs, and he sat listening to her boots on the treads until the sound gave out.

story:
Maxime had told everyone at school that he volunteered all the time, which was true if you counted the one afternoon in grade ten when he'd sorted bottles for an hour, so when his guidance counsellor slid the form across the desk he signed it mostly to keep the story alive. The form said Riverside Seniors' Residence, Saturday, nine o'clock, warehouse side entrance. He imagined a line of grateful people, imagined himself handing over bags of pasta with an easy smile, the kind of smile he had never in his life managed on command.

The warehouse turned out to be exactly what it said: a warehouse. A woman named Delphine gave him a clipboard and pointed at pallets of canned tomatoes, and for two hours he counted and logged, entirely alone except for a radio playing something French his grandmother might have liked. Nobody came for groceries. At ten he went to find Delphine, trying to sound casual rather than lost. "So when do the people start arriving?"

She looked at him the way you look at a shoe on the wrong foot. "Nobody picks up food here. This is the food bank. A food bank is a central warehouse that collects and distributes food to local agencies, while a food pantry is where people pick up food directly." She said it flat, the way you say something you've said forty times, and turned back to her manifest.

So the seniors' residence, he learned, was one of the agencies. The pantry ran out of the common room on the ground floor, between the fish tank and the piano nobody played, and Delphine drove him over at eleven in a van that smelled of cardboard and oranges. Maxime sat with the clipboard on his knees and thought about how he'd described his morning to himself that morning, competent, experienced, practically a veteran of charity work, and how none of that had been true, and how the false version had still gotten him into the van. Both things seemed to hold at once, and he didn't try to sort them out before they arrived.

The common room had been rearranged so the shelves formed a narrow aisle, and by noon there was a queue of residents and people from the neighbourhood pushing walkers or carrying folded bags. An old man named Armand expostulated loudly about the disappearance of the good biscuits, holding up a box of generic ones as evidence, until the woman running the shelf, Madame Roy, told him that the good biscuits would return when the donations turned over, which was a way of saying maybe never. Armand took the generic ones anyway. Maxime watched him choose to accept it, and understood that accepting things was maybe also a skill, one he had not been tested on yet.

He was put on bread. A girl from another school, Noor, worked beside him, and she was faster, and she knew residents by name. When he mentioned the warehouse and how he'd expected crowds, she laughed without unkindness. "Everyone thinks that the first time," she said. "That the big building is where it happens." But it was where it happened, he thought, or half of it; the pallets he'd counted that morning were becoming, at this table, the exact number of loaves now going into bags. His counting had been real. It had just been real somewhere else.

The afternoon had a rhythm he hadn't expected, conversations that started about bread and ended up elsewhere. A resident named Gisèle told him the period after the residence's old activities coordinator quit had been what she called an interregnum, months of nothing scheduled, and how the pantry had filled the empty afternoons even for people who didn't need the food. She took two loaves though she needed both, so he didn't argue with the second half of her sentence. He was beginning to suspect that people carried more than one reason for most things they did, and that his own two reasons, the story for school and something under it he couldn't yet name, were not so different.

At four they closed the shelves. Noor left quickly, waving. Delphine appeared in the doorway with paperwork, and Gisèle, waiting for her elevator, told Maxime that afternoons like this one were evanescent and that he should not bother holding on to them, since they vanished no matter how tightly you gripped, and the vanishing was the part that made them worth having. He wanted to tell her he'd be back next Saturday, but he wasn't sure yet whether that was true or just the next version of the story he told, so he said he'd see, and she nodded as if that were the most honest answer in the building.

He rode back to the warehouse with Delphine, logging returns in the fading light. On Monday he would tell his friends he ran a pantry, or worked at a food bank, or something in between, and whichever words he chose would be partly true. For now there were thirty-one cans of tomatoes left on the pallet, and the clipboard, and his own handwriting from that morning, which looked, he noticed, exactly like the handwriting of someone who had done this before.

"Same time next week?" Delphine asked, not looking up.

He clicked the pen twice. "Yeah. Same time."

Aiden signed in at the folding table by the garden gate and wrote his name under a column of volunteers he did not recognize. The coordinator, a woman named Marisol with dirt under her fingernails, handed him a pair of gloves and pointed at the raised beds along the fence. "Tomatoes and zucchini today. Whatever's ripe goes into the crates, crates go to the tent at noon." She said it the way someone says a thing they have said four hundred times.

The food bank itself had been set up under a white canopy at the far end of the lot, beside the tool shed. Aiden had expected a short weekday line, maybe a dozen people, the way his mother described the drop-in center near her office. By eleven the line ran past the compost bins and along the whole south fence. He counted to forty and stopped.

"I know," said the volunteer next to him, a boy called Theo who went to the Catholic school and wore an ascetic sort of outfit, plain grey shirt, plain grey pants, as though he had decided against owning anything decorative. "First time?" Aiden nodded. Theo pulled a folded page from his pocket, a printout of something called HungerCount 2025, and smoothed it against his knee. "Food Banks Canada did the count. Nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025. A record for a single month." He said the last part flatly, like a verdict.

"Two point two million people," Aiden said.

"Visits. Not people. One person can come twice, three times." Theo folded the page again. "Somebody coming back every month isn't four different people."

Aiden turned that over while he picked zucchini. His mother was a pragmatist about this kind of thing. She donated, she said, because charity worked faster than politics, and you gave where the pipeline was shortest, and you did not agonize. His father, on the rare evenings he still came to dinner, took the opposite view and would excoriate the government over his plate, though he had never once driven Aiden anywhere to volunteer. Aiden had always assumed he would land on one side eventually, the way people apparently did.

Marisol came down the row with an empty crate and started picking on the other side of the plants. "Theo's got his numbers out again," she said.

"They're the real numbers."

"I know they're real." She snapped a tomato off its stem. "I also know we fed three hundred and ten families out of this garden last year, and none of them cared about the statistics while they were eating."

"That's not a counterargument," Theo said.

"It's not an argument. It's a crate of tomatoes."

Aiden kept his head down and his hands moving. Both of them were right in a way that did not add up, or added up to something he could not name yet. The numbers said the problem was larger than any garden, and the garden was right there, feeding people Theo would never meet, at noon, regardless of what anyone said at a dinner table. Maybe the honest position was holding both at once without pretending they reconciled. He did not say this out loud. He was not sure it survived being said.

At noon he carried the crates to the tent. A woman with a clipboard was checking people in, and the line moved slowly, bag by bag, and Aiden's job was to hand each household their vegetables and say the amount, two zucchini, one pint of tomatoes, until the crates were low. Then he looked up and saw Mr. Palek, his grade nine geography teacher, the one who had once kept Aiden after class to tell him he thought too much and should try joining something. Mr. Palek wore a jacket Aiden recognized from school, and he stood with his hands in his pockets, three people from the front.

"Aiden," Mr. Palek said, and then, quickly, "I'm picking up for my sister. She's got the flu."

"Sure," Aiden said. He handed over the zucchini and the tomatoes and said the amounts the way he had said them to everyone else, because it seemed worse somehow to do otherwise. Mr. Palek took the bag, and his hand stayed a moment on the crate's edge.

"Good to see you joined something," he said.

Aiden watched him walk back down the row with the bag held against his chest, past the compost bins, past the fence, until he turned onto the street and was gone. Theo appeared beside him with the last crate.

"You okay?"

"Yeah," Aiden said. He took the crate and carried it to the table. "Two zucchini, one pint of tomatoes."

Noemie arrived at Marlane Lanes eleven minutes early, which she decided was a mistake the moment she walked in, because it gave her time to stand under the fluorescent lights rehearsing everything she might say to a boy she had only ever spoken to through a screen. His name was Deegan. He had transferred into her AP Gov class in March and sat one row over, and for three weeks they had argued about gerrymandering in the class forum with what she suspected was mutual, deliberate slowness to concede points. Then a message that was not about gerrymandering at all. Then this. She rented shoes, size seven, and took a lane by the window where she could watch the parking lot.

He came in carrying two large sodas from the concession stand, one in each hand, which she understood immediately as an act of preempt kindness, a way of skipping the awkward first transaction of who pays for what. She stood up to wave. The front of his shoe caught on the lip where the carpet met the lane approach, and both cups went up and out of him like he was releasing birds. Cola arced across the scoring table, pooled in the gutter of the ball return, and soaked the left leg of his jeans from thigh to shin.

"Oh no," Noemie said, and then, because there was nothing else to do, she started laughing, and then covered her mouth in horror at herself.

"I just," Deegan said, standing very still in the puddle, "ruined everything. Before hello. I ruined everything before hello." He was not laughing. He was looking at the sodas lying on their sides with their straws still in them, and his ears had gone a color she had never seen on a person before.

They got paper towels from the desk, and the man behind the counter brought a mop without being asked, with the weary competence of someone who had done this before, and Deegan apologized to the mop man and to Noemie and, briefly, to the sodas. Noemie found that she was not bored or embarrassed for him. She kept catching the wet stripe on his leg and feeling something warm and unhelpful in her chest, which she distrusted, because she had spent eighteen years assembling a working theory that competence was the only thing worth admiring. She had chosen her college, her summer job, her friendships, on that theory. Deegan mopping his own leg with a scratchy brown towel should have lowered him in her estimation. It did not.

"Okay," she said when they were seated and mostly dry, "tell me something true." It was a game she played, and she knew it was a slightly aggressive way to open a date, a trap dressed as a game, a small test of mendacity. Deegan considered her for a long second, which she liked better than a fast answer.

"I'm afraid of the ball return," he said. "Genuinely. I think my hand is going to get crushed. I've been afraid of it since I was seven. Also I looked you up before I asked you out, and your debate videos are online, and you're better at that than anyone I've ever seen in person." He said it flatly, without flattery's usual lean.

She took her turn, picked up the eight-pound ball she had chosen, and stood at the line thinking about the videos, which she watched alone at night with her hand over her mouth, and about how nobody ever saw the take where she forgot her rebuttal entirely and sat frozen for forty seconds. She bowled a strike without planning to. When she came back he was grinning at her, and she heard herself say, "There was this experiment in 1966. Elliot Aronson. This contestant who was really good at a quiz spilled a cup of coffee, and people rated him more likable afterward. It's called the pratfall effect."

"Did you just cite a study at me instead of saying you like me?"

"Maybe those are the same sentence," she said, and felt her face go the color of his ears. "The coffee thing only worked because he was competent first, though. That's the part I can't tell. Whether I'm allowed to spill." She rolled the ball again and got seven pins, and Deegan said he would take the finger-crushing lane position if she never told anyone, and she said nothing, which was its own answer, and slid the scoring sheet toward him to write his own name.

The marquee said 7:15, and it was already 7:09, so Faith stopped pretending to read the posters and bought the tickets herself, fast, before Ethan could reach for his wallet and make it a thing. The movie was called The Drowning Hour, a pelagic horror her brother had described as two hours of open water and one shark, and she had chosen it, which she kept repeating to herself like an alibi. She was calm. She was, historically, the calm one, the girl her brother called a misanthrope mostly because she'd never brought anyone home, and she was calm now, holding two tickets while Ethan jogged up the theater steps with his backpack bouncing.

"Sorry, sorry. Bus." He was out of breath. His hair was wet. She noted all of this and concluded nothing, because concluding things was how people got things wrong, and she was not going to get this wrong.

Dez was working concessions, which was either luck or the opposite. Dez had been her best friend since sixth grade and had opinions she dispensed like napkins. "The Drowning Hour," Dez said, filling their popcorn. "Bold choice for a first date. There was this study, right, my psych teacher mentioned it. 1974. These two guys, Dutton and Aron. Men who'd just crossed a scary suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy one."

"Call her how?" Ethan asked.

"They had her number. They called her." Dez shrugged. "Scared hearts get mixed up with liking people. Have a great movie."

Faith laughed, the dismissive laugh she used on Dez, and did not think about it again for approximately forty minutes. That was a lie she told herself later. She thought about it while the previews ran. She thought about it while Ethan settled into his seat with a full centimeter of space between their arms, a centimeter she kept measuring like it was a border dispute. Her heart was doing something in her chest, a quick insistent drumming, and she catalogued it honestly: was that Ethan, or was it the dark, or the fact that she'd eaten nothing since noon?

The first hour of the movie was almost entirely water. A woman on a research vessel, alone, a radio that cut in and out, and a shape under the surface that the camera refused to show properly, which was the whole trick of it. When the shape finally surfaced, Faith's whole body reacted before her mind could file paperwork, and Ethan made a sound, a short vowel, and gripped the armrest, and she found his hand there without deciding to. Her palm was sweating. So was his. Neither of them pulled away.

Here is what she did not tell herself, and what she would only admit on the walk home: she had known, for eleven days, that Ethan had asked out Marina first. Marina had told her at lunch, laughing, saying he'd texted her some paragraph about her eyes, and Marina had said no. Eleven days of knowing, and she'd said yes to the same paragraph, lightly edited, and she had narrated the whole evening as if the knowledge didn't exist. Dez knew too. That was why the story about the bridges, told with those particular eyes on Faith's face while Faith pretended to watch the butter drizzle. Dez had been trying to disenfranchise the lie, take away its vote before it could be counted.

But that wasn't the pounding, either, or not only. On the screen the woman was treading water in the dark, talking to herself to stay awake, and Faith sat with the two feelings side by side and refused to merge them, because the study men had crossed one bridge and felt one thing and called it something, and she had crossed two bridges at once, the old lie and the new hand, and no study covered that. Maybe she liked Ethan. Maybe she liked being chosen. Maybe she was scared of the water and scared of Marina finding out and scared in some way she didn't have a word for, and the honest position was that she did not know, and that not knowing was survivable, which was itself a finding.

The credits came up. The house lights didn't, not right away, and they sat in the dark with their hands still together, both pretending to read the credits.

"So," Ethan said. "Did you like it?"

Outside it had started raining, thin and silver under the streetlights, and the last bus she could catch was in six minutes. Faith looked at their hands, then at him.

"Dez thinks I only think I like you because I'm scared," she said.

Ethan was quiet for a moment. "Are you?"

She pulled him toward the doors, into the rain, running for the bus with the tickets still crumpled in her pocket, and shouted over her shoulder, "Ask me after the sturdy bridge."

The break room clipboard had a new sheet taped to it on Tuesday: the store's contract with Local 304 expired in six weeks, and anyone with questions about negotiations should talk to Dez, the steward who worked the deli counter. Sadie read it twice while her soup went cold, mostly because her paycheck that week had been 40 percent smaller than the last one. Her hours had been cut from twenty-eight to sixteen, just under the line where the contract required the store to keep her on the schedule, and nobody had explained why the line existed or who had drawn it.

She found Dez slicing turkey an hour before close. "Why do I even pay union dues," Sadie asked, "if they can cut my hours anyway?" Dez kept the blade steady. "Dues are eleven a pay period. You make three dollars an hour more than the starting rate at the non-union place on Route 9, you get time-and-a-half on Sundays, and they can't schedule you past ten on a school night. That's the contract. It's not magic, it's a deal we renegotiate, and right now it's up." Sadie said she hadn't known it was a deal. "Everything's a deal," Dez said. "Some deals you just weren't in the room for."

Sadie had thought of the union the way she thought of the fire sprinklers, something installed before she arrived. Her father, who drove a delivery truck and had been through two contract fights, talked about it differently, but he tended to valorize the picket line so heavily that she stopped listening halfway through. She wanted the numbers. On Thursday she took the contract binder from the office shelf while the assistant manager was on the lot and copied the wage scale into her phone: year one, year two, the differentials for nights and Sundays, the grievance procedure, all of it written down and enforceable, which was more than her friend Tessa had at the coffee shop, where the manager decided everything on mood.

That was the week Rosa got called in. Rosa worked the bakery, twenty years in, and the new store director, Mr. Kranz, had been circling her about the broken proofer and a Saturday when the case had been left half stocked. He came out to the bakery floor at 4:30 and said, "Rosa, come to my office in ten minutes. Just a conversation." Rosa wiped her hands on her aprs and looked at Dez across the store, then at Sadie, who was nearest the register.

"That's not just a conversation," Rosa said quietly. "If he writes me up for that Saturday, I lose the overtime differential for ninety days."

"You can bring someone," Sadie said. She had read it the night before, on the third page of the new-hire orientation folder nobody had walked her through, under a heading she'd had to read twice. "It's a Supreme Court thing. NLRB v. J. Weingarten, 1975. Unionized workers may request a union representative at an interview they reasonably believe could lead to discipline." She'd found it because she'd been reading the binder cover to cover, looking for the hours clause, and had stopped on that page long enough for it to stick.

Rosa went to the office with Dez. Sadie covered the bakery case for twenty minutes, sliding the day-old bread to the discount rack, restocking the rolls. When they came out, Dez's expression gave nothing away. "He asked his questions, I sat there, Rosa answered the ones she wanted to answer," Dez said. "He wanted it to be informal. Informal goes one direction." Rosa straightened her hat. "He said the proofer is my responsibility. I said write down what I'm responsible for and I'll sign it. He didn't write it down."

Sadie thought about that on the bus home, her phone open to the payroll app, checking whether the new schedule had posted. It had: sixteen hours again. She understood now that the contract was the reason she wasn't at twelve, and that the coming negotiations were the reason she might be at twenty-four, and that her dues and her Sunday rate and Rosa's right to have someone in the room all came from the same slow machinery, which worked but never all the way, the way an asymptote never touches its line. She also understood that she had exactly no leverage alone, and some leverage together, and that "together" meant showing up to meetings she had skipped all summer. It was not, she was honest enough to admit, an altruistic feeling. She wanted her hours back. It just happened that the road to her hours ran through everyone else's.

The union meeting was Sunday night in the library basement, folding chairs and a card table with a coffee urn. Sadie signed the attendance sheet, took a chair in the back, and raised her hand before she could talk herself out of it.

"I'm Sadie. Front end. I want to say something about the hours clause."

The table had been moved to the middle of Aunt Carol's living room so that everyone could fit, and Evan's grandfather sat at the head of it with his fork held like a conductor's baton, waiting for someone to mention music. He did this at every family dinner, and every family dinner someone eventually obliged, because refusing him was harder than playing along. Tonight Evan had decided he would be the one to oblige. He had also decided, somewhere between the salad and the pot roast, that he was a coward, because his flight to Boston left at eleven tomorrow morning and he had not yet said the thing the dinner was supposedly celebrating.

"Your school played the Elgar at graduation," his grandfather said, pointing the fork at Evan. "The March Number One. You probably didn't know what it was."

"I knew," Evan said. "Pomp and Circumstance."

His grandfather's face opened like a window. He set the fork down. He was, Evan's mother liked to say, a connoisseur of old recordings, which meant the den shelves were full of records nobody was allowed to touch, and he could tell you which orchestra, which year, which horn flubbed the eighth bar. "Do you know where Elgar got the title?"

"From somewhere," Evan said, carefully, because he did know, and knowing was the whole problem. Mrs. Adeyemi had made them read Othello in the spring, and when the band began the processional in the gymnasium, the phrase had surfaced in his head like a fish rising, pride, pomp and circumstance of glorious war, and he had stood there in his rented gown feeling like he'd been handed a message he wasn't sure he wanted.

Nobody at the table knew. His uncle guessed a king's funeral. His cousin guessed the Bible, which made his grandfather flinch. "Take a guess," his grandfather said to Evan, and Evan looked at the cake waiting on the sideboard, at the clock over the stove that said 7:40, at his mother who kept glancing at him because she knew what he had not said and knew the car to the airport would come for his grandfather at nine, sharp, always sharp, a man who had served twenty-six years and did not miss planes.

"Othello," Evan said. "Elgar took the title from Othello. The play mentions the 'pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war.'"

The table went quiet in the way it did when the youngest person said something the oldest person didn't expect. His grandfather leaned back. "You read it in school."

"Second semester. English." Evan turned his water glass a quarter turn on the tablecloth. "It's Othello's speech. He's talking about losing his profession, the thing that made him who he is." He hadn't planned to say the next part, but the clock and the roast and the whole assembled family made a corridor he had to walk down. "Grandpa, I turned down the academy. The appointment. I mailed the letter Thursday. I'm going to Boston in the fall for engineering."

His grandfather's hand found the edge of the table and stayed there. The kitchen fan hummed. Somebody's chair creaked. Through the window the boreal light of late June still lay across the yard, pale and slow to leave, so that it didn't feel like evening even though it was.

"Forty-one years I went to ceremonies with that march," his grandfather said finally. "Eleven of them for men who got flags instead of diplomas." He picked up the fork again and set it down again. "You're saying I've been listening to a war speech at every graduation in this country."

"I'm saying it's about both. The pomp is real and the pomp costs something." Evan heard himself stop, which was new for him; in school he would have kept going, interpolated the counterargument about service and duty and family the way you patch a sentence to be safe. "I'm not sure I'm right. I'm sure I couldn't do it your way, and I couldn't do it halfway, so."

"So you chose the other thing entirely." His grandfather looked at the cake, then at Evan's mother, then back at the window, where the light was finally beginning to go. "Your grandmother would have said you argue like a Jesuit." He pushed his chair back. "Come outside before the car comes. Help an old man find his cigars."

Evan followed him out into the last of the pale evening, and his grandfather sat down on the porch step and patted the place beside him.

The walk-in door slammed and Chef's voice carried over the fryers before Kyle had even set down the tub of romaine. "Kyle, station four, you're on apps tonight, not salads." Kyle pulled his apron tight and said nothing. At the pass, two men he didn't recognize sat with Miriam, the lead line cook, one of them sliding a yellow card across the steel counter. Kyle caught the words as he passed: collective bargaining, bargaining unit, election date.

"He's busting hours again," Miriam was saying. "Nate closed six nights last week. Overtime on the books, then the hours get corrected." The older of the two visitors, the one with the yellow card, nodded and wrote. Kyle diced shallots and listened. His own schedule had swung from eighteen hours a week to thirty-four and back since June, and when he'd asked about the difference, the manager had shrugged and said scheduling was a business decision.

The younger visitor came over while Kyle waited on a delivery at the back dock. "You full time here?" he asked. "Part time, but full hours most weeks," Kyle said. "Then you'd be in the unit, depending how the cards fall. Name's Deshawn, by the way." He talked about wage scales, about grievance procedures, about how the National Labor Relations Act backed up the whole structure. Kyle said his cousin Marcus worked at the post office and made time and a half on Sundays, and Deshawn smiled.

That summer at the Halloway farm came back to him whole: the flat Kansas light, the eighty-hour weeks at flat pay, the water jug by the tomato rows. Marcus had come through on his way to a training in Topeka, sitting on the tailgate in his postal uniform, and Kyle had asked him why the farm crew couldn't do what his local did. "We're not covered," Ramón, the crew boss, had cut in, before Marcus could answer. Marcus had nodded slowly. "The Act doesn't cover agricultural workers," he said. "Or government employees, domestic workers, supervisors, independent contractors." He'd counted them on his fingers, like a list he'd memorized for a test. "Everyone else, mostly, they can organize under it. You guys, no."

Kyle had thought Marcus was wrong. He'd gone to the library in town and asked, and the librarian had pulled the statute and turned to the section on coverage, and there it was in print, exclusions plain as a fence line. He'd photocopied the page and left it folded in Ramón's truck, and Ramón had let it sit on the dashboard all season, untouched, sun-faded by August, as if keeping it visible were the only use for it.

Back on the line, the ticket printer chattered and Kyle plated six crab stacks without a pause. During the lull, Nate came by the apps station, wiping his hands. "You gonna sign one of those cards?" Kyle asked him quietly. Nate's jaw worked. "I got an interview at the county garage Thursday. City job. Different rules, I guess." He said it flat, and Kyle understood that Nate hadn't known either, until this week, that the law covering the kitchen and the law covering a government garage weren't the same law at all.

Deshawn returned to the dock with a clipboard, and Kyle asked him the thing he'd been chewing since the farm. "If the Act covers us here, why not farmworkers? Who drew that line?" Deshawn shrugged, unbothered, almost cheerful. "People fought over every word of that thing. You want clean, you're in the wrong business." Kyle thought of Ramón's truculent silence at the union meeting that two kids from the county had tried to organize in July, the way the whole crew had let one loud man's contempt decide for all of them, since the law gave them no ground to stand on anyway. He thought of Marcus's fingers counting out the excluded. It wasn't casuistry, he decided, the distinction between the kitchen and the field; it was just a line, drawn somewhere, by someone, and a man could denigrate it all he wanted and still have to work on whichever side of it he'd been born.

He signed the card at the end of shift, printing his name in the box for bargaining unit employees. His hand stopped over the line asking his classification, hourly and title, and he looked up at Deshawn. "What if they call me a supervisor after this?" Deshawn took the clipboard back, tapped it once against the doorframe, and grinned. "Then we find out what they think you are."

Kyle slid the card across the counter to Miriam, and she put it in her shirt pocket without looking at it. "Eighty-six the crab, we're out," Chef shouted, and Kyle turned back to the burners.

The portal refreshed to the same gray screen it had shown all morning, the one that said his application remained under review, and Logan pulled his hands off the keyboard before he could hit reload again. It was a Saturday in March, the last Saturday before the decisions were supposed to come out, and he had promised himself he would only check twice a day. He had already broken the promise four times since breakfast.

His mother called something up from the kitchen about lunch, and he answered without turning around, because the email tab had just flashed. It was a coupon. He sat with his disappointment for a second, then noticed his little sister leaning in the doorway, watching him with the particular patience of someone who wanted the computer.

"You can have it in a minute," he said. "I'm waiting on something."

"A college thing?"

"A college thing."

Maya came and stood behind his chair, chewing the end of her braid the way she did when she was deciding whether to be annoying. Instead she asked him which one he wanted, and he started to say the obvious answer, the one he'd been saying since December, and then stopped, because the honest answer had gotten complicated.

He had visited the campus in October with his dad. The tour guide, a senior in a rain jacket the school's exact shade of blue, had walked them past the library and said, almost as a boast, that the place had one of the highest yields in the country. A kid near the back, some other senior on the tour, had raised a hand and asked what that meant. "Yield," the guide said, "is the percentage of students we admit who actually accept the offer and enroll." Logan had written it in his phone, partly because it sounded like something he should know, and partly because the way she said it, proud and casual at once, had struck him as strange. She wasn't talking about learning anything. She was talking about being chosen, and choosing, as if the two were the same act.

Afterward, at dinner, his dad had called the school a good investment, talked about recuperating the cost of tuition over a working lifetime, and Logan had nodded while feeling that the word fit badly, like a shirt borrowed from someone bigger. What he remembered from the tour wasn't the ranking or the food or the tour guide's boast. It was the basement of the engineering building, where a grad student had shown them a modular robotics lab, and had used the word modularity the way other people said hello, casually, constantly, as though the world were obviously made of parts that could be swapped. Logan had spent the whole walk back to the car imagining himself there, alone at a bench at midnight, the subterranean hum of the ventilation the only sound. That was the school he wanted. He was almost sure.

But there was the other one, the state school forty minutes away, where his best friend Dara was already enrolled, and where his mother had quietly started saying things like close enough to come home for dinner. Dara had texted him that morning: checking yet. He typed checking yet back, deleted it, and typed a real answer instead. The truth was that he had two pictures of himself and no way to make them one picture. At the far school he would be built from new parts. At the near one he would keep his old parts, and his family, and Sunday dinners, and the version of himself that Dara already knew how to talk to.

"You're doing the face," Maya said.

"What face?"

"The one where you're arguing with somebody who isn't there."

He laughed, which he hadn't done all day, and slid out of the chair. "It's yours."

She climbed into it and opened a game, and he stood behind her for a moment with his hands in his pockets, then walked to the kitchen, where his mother was slicing a pear. Out the window the neighbor's magnolia had started, weeks early, its buds splitting into white. His phone buzzed against his leg before he reached the table.

Dara again: whatever the email says, call me first.

"Is that the college?" his mother asked, not looking up from the knife.

"Not yet," Logan said, and put the phone face down on the counter, and reached past her for the good end of the pear.

story:
The new warm-up arrived on a laminated sheet taped to the gym door, and by the third day of it half the team had opinions. Laurie's opinion, offered while hopping on one leg in a squat at midcourt, was that whoever invented it had never tried to do it at six a.m. "This is not a warm-up," said Priya, wobbling beside her. "This is a audition for a flamingo documentary." The routine went on for twenty minutes: single-leg squats, then jumps where you had to land soft with your knees bent, then cutting drills where you planted a foot and changed direction on command, like the floor was lava and the coach held the map.

Friday was the season opener against Delbrook, and Coach Renner had declared that nobody who skipped the warm-up played a minute, which gave the whole week the feeling of a hostage negotiation conducted in jump rope. Dana, the senior point guard, led the resistance. She would do the drills, but sarcastically, sighing like a Victorian widow at each landing, and she had begun referring to the routine as "the ritual" in a voice that suggested druids. "My grandmother warmed up with a cigarette and a stretch of the hamstrings," Dana announced on Wednesday, "and she lived to ninety-one." "Her knees," said Priya, "did not."

Laurie had torn nothing, but she remembered Kayla Mott, two years ahead of her, who had planted to cut in a January game and gone down before any defender touched her, her knee simply declining the assignment. Laurie had been in the bleachers that night, fourteen years old, hearing the specific sound the gym made when three hundred people went quiet at once. Kayla had come back the next season, braced and careful, and Laurie had once watched her pause at the top of the key, in an open gym with nobody within ten feet, and pass up the drive she would have taken as a sophomore. That memory sat with Laurie while she did her flamingo squats, and she didn't like where it sat.

So while the rest of the team filed out for water, Laurie peeled the laminated sheet off the door and actually read it, instead of skimming for the part where the suffering ended. It was more prolix than it needed to be, a small ocean of paragraphs about session structure and progression, but she collated what mattered: the drills weren't random humiliation. They trained balance, landing technique, and how you cut and change direction. And the sheet said, in a sentence so plain it was almost shy, that programs like this had been shown to reduce the risk of knee ligament injuries. Ligaments, plural, meaning the things that held knees together, meaning the thing that had happened to Kayla without anyone touching her.

"Are you reading the flyer," Dana said, returning with her water bottle, "for fun." "For information," Laurie said. "It says the routine cuts the risk of knee ligament injuries. That's the whole point. It's not Coach punishing us for being young." Dana squinted at the sheet as if it might be forged. "The flyer would say that. The flyer is pro-warm-up propaganda." "It's not propaganda if it's true," Laurie said. "That's just facts." Dana considered this with the gravity of a Supreme Court. "Then they should have led with that," she said. "A sentence like that on the door, and none of the fifty paragraphs." Laurie admitted the flyer's authors would have benefited from an epigram or two, and Dana, who kept a notebook of coach quotes for exactly this purpose, promised to write one: "Bend your knees, keep your future."

By Thursday the resistance had not exactly surrendered but had negotiated terms. Dana performed the landings loudly but correctly, knees out, chest up, and when the youngest player, Beatrix, asked why they were jumping onto a box and then off it like nervous cats, it was Dana, not the trainer, who said, "Balance, landing, cutting. It protects your knees, kid." Laurie suspected Dana of enjoying the authority more than the science, but the result was the same: Beatrix stopped asking to skip it, and Priya stopped narrating the flamingo documentary, except for special occasions.

Laurie herself had arrived somewhere she could not fully pin down. She did the routine properly now, not because the flyer had converted her in a single reading, but because she had weighed the twenty boring minutes against the memory of Kayla pausing at the top of the key, and found the math easy. Still, she was honest with herself about the residue of doubt: nothing in the program guaranteed anything; risk was reduced, not erased, and a bad plant could still end a season in a gym that went quiet. She decided she could live with that arithmetic, and also that she would rather do the arithmetic than not know it existed.

On Friday they lost to Delbrook by four, in a game with three bad bounces and one moment where Laurie planted, cut, and felt her knee take the turn like a promissory note. She finished the game, showered, and found Dana by the doors, icing a bruised hip and looking unbearably pleased. "The ritual claims another survivor," Laurie said. Dana held up her notebook, open to a fresh page. "New epigram. 'Soft landings, long careers.'" She tapped the pen against it twice. "I'm workshopping."

story:
Hailey's uncle Rick arrived at the graduation barbecue with a store-bought pie and the air of a man who had rehearsed something in the car. He found her on the porch steps, still wearing her gown because her mother had wanted photos in every corner of the yard, including, for reasons unclear, beside the compost bin. "Nineteen dollars a week," Rick said, handing her a slice of pie before she'd asked for one. "Actually, hold on. That's not the number. Let me get it right, I looked it up this morning."

"Get what right?"

"Your diploma." He sat down beside her, balancing his own plate on his knee. "In 2023, workers twenty-five and older with a high school diploma had median weekly earnings of eight hundred ninety-nine dollars. Without one, seven hundred eight. Your grandmother wants me to make a toast later and I refuse to be vague about it."

Hailey chewed and did the subtraction in her head, then did it again because the first answer felt too tidy. A hundred ninety-one dollars a week, and she was pretty sure her grandmother's toaster cost less than that. She said nothing, because Rick was already drifting toward the cooler, and because her cousin Devi had just commandeered the porch railing as a photo backdrop and was directing people like a small, stubborn air traffic controller.

Later, when the burgers had been eaten and the dogs had been fed illegal scraps, Hailey borrowed her mother's laptop at the kitchen table and checked. There it was, the same numbers Rick had recited, sitting in a government table as calmly as a fact about rainfall. Median weekly earnings, workers twenty-five and over: $899 with a diploma, $708 without. She had assumed the diploma mattered, of course, the way you assume vitamins matter, without ever seeing the label. Here was the label. She sat with her hand on the trackpad while the screen dimmed and then brightened again when she moved.

"You're doing homework at your own party," Devi said, leaning over her shoulder with a cup of lemonade. "That's the saddest thing I've seen all day, and I watched Grandpa debate the potato salad."

"I'm doing math. If I work from now until I'm twenty-five with just this, versus if I'd quit, it's, like, a real amount of money. It's a car. It's several cars."

"It's imaginary cars. You were never going to quit."

"That's not the point. The point is it has a price. I keep thinking of it as, I don't know, a piece of paper shaped like an accomplishment."

"An ideologue would say the diploma is about learning, not wages," Devi said, in her impression of their tenth-grade history teacher, which involved narrowing her eyes and going slightly nasal. "A cynic would say it's a tollbooth. You're allowed to be both, I think. Grandpa is both and he's the happiest person here."

Out in the yard, Grandpa was indeed both, in the sedimentary way of a man who had accumulated opinions in distinct layers over eighty years and let them sit peacefully on top of one another. He waved his fork at the graduates, all four of them lined up in their gowns like migrating birds, and announced that education was either the great equalizer or a very expensive piece of felt, depending on the day.

Hailey carried the laptop outside, because the light was going amber and her mother would want the last photos before it failed entirely. The gown was too warm now, smelling faintly of other people's houses and her own deodorant losing its argument with the afternoon. Her mother positioned her under the maple and said "chin up, no, the other chin, there," and took eleven pictures, of which two would survive.

Rick made his toast at dusk, standing on a cooler. He got the numbers right again, both of them, and raised his glass, and everyone raised their cups, including the dogs in spirit. Then Hailey's aunt yelled from the porch that the pie was running out, and the toast dissolved into a stampede, and Hailey stood alone for a moment in the middle of the yard, diploma rolled under her arm like a baton she hadn't decided to run with yet. Devi appeared beside her, held out the last slice on a napkin, and said, "So what's it worth?"

Hailey took the slice and considered it, and the question, and the maple, and her mother laughing at something with her whole body. "More than pie," she said. "Ask me in eight years."

story:
I had the whole afternoon planned, and I want it on record that nothing that went wrong was my fault. The AP studio critique was at three o'clock, which gave me ninety minutes to finish the painting I had told everyone, including Ms. Okafor, was already finished. In fairness to me, it had been finished on Tuesday. It was only this morning, passing the storage rack, that I had seen Samira's piece drying there, all those clean saturated bands of color, and understood that mine was gray where it should have been loud.

The problem was a single area, the isthmus of pale ground between the two halves of my composition, a narrow land bridge of canvas I had left bare on purpose. The painting showed my grandmother's kitchen and, across the divide, the airport gate where I had last hugged her, and I had intended to fill that strip with a bright impossible gold, the color of the two places touching. I squeezed out cadmium yellow, a worm of it, and added white. Too chalky. I added orange. Warmer, but duller. A drop of red, then a little blue to cool it back, then more yellow to recover what the blue had eaten, and I worked the palette knife in small circles as though persistence alone could suture the color back to brightness.

Instead the mixture slid toward brown. Not a rich, deliberate brown, but the flat brown of puddle water, and the more pigments I folded in the darker and muddier it got. I stood there with the knife going around and around, telling myself it would turn if I only found the right tube, which is a thing I apparently still believe about paint at eighteen.

Across the table, Priya was washing her brushes at the sink, uninvolved and unhurried. "What happened to your gold?"

"I'm getting there," I said.

"You're not, though. Mr. Ruiz said this last week and you weren't listening. Mixing paint is subtractive." She dried a brush on her jeans. "Light does the other thing. Paint isn't light."

I almost argued with her, and then I didn't, because the brown on my knife was its own argument. I set it down and looked at the palette, at the graveyard of half-mixed dabs, and turned the idea over the way you turn a coin. Light mixes by adding; paint mixes by taking away. Every pigment I layered in was another substance absorbing its share of the wavelengths, so the more of them I combined, the less light any of them could give back. A hundred colors stacked together wouldn't climb toward white. They would sink toward this. Toward mud.

Priya had gone back to her own piece, so I sat alone with it. My first instinct, honestly, was to hide the brown, to paint over the strip and pretend the gold had never been the plan. That was the version of myself I'd been narrating all semester, the one whose paintings arrived whole. But there was another way to think, and it belonged to my grandmother, who never wasted anything: she quilted with the leftovers of other projects, saved every selvage, called scraps of fabric "the memory of the dress." Waste was profligate to her, almost a sin, but accident was not waste. Accident was material.

So I stopped trying to make the gold and used the brown. I laid it into the strip in short horizontal strokes, letting the muddy color sit between the kitchen and the gate, and then I dragged a single unbroken line of pure cadmium through the center of it, straight from the tube, mixed with nothing, so it sang the way yellow only sings when it's alone. The two sides of the painting no longer blended into each other. They faced each other across the brown, connected by one bright seam.

At three o'clock we pinned everything to the wall. Ms. Okafor stood in front of mine for a long time, arms folded, and Samira leaned in beside her. "The center is different," Samira said. "It was empty before."

"It's the bridge," I said, and then, more quietly, because it was the truth and I hadn't decided yet whether to spend the truth in public, "it's also every mistake I made this afternoon, all in one place."

Ms. Okafor asked whether the seam of yellow was a decision or a rescue. I told her it was a decision. Then I told her it was a rescue. She wrote something on her clipboard, and I watched the yellow line catch the fluorescent light and hold it, and I did not ask what she had written.

story:
Maika signed her name twice on the hiring form, once as employee and once as the minor whose parent also had to sign, and the woman at the counter slid a laminated card across the glass. "You're sixteen, so there are certain stations you can't work," the woman said. "It's federal. Under US child labor rules, workers under 18 can't operate power-driven meat slicers. Doesn't matter if it's a grocery store deli or a restaurant. The rule is the rule." Maika folded the card into her back pocket and followed the woman through the swinging doors into the back of the store, where the air smelled of vinegar and cold plastic.

The manager, Mr. Voss, was a saturnine man who moved through the aisles like weather, and he handed her a broom before he handed her a schedule. "Sweep the deli floor, wipe the case, bag the olives," he said. "You don't touch the slicer." He pointed at it anyway, the steel disc catching the fluorescent light, and Maika nodded as though she were internalizing a religion rather than a restriction, the kind of thing you obeyed before you understood it.

Her first shift ended at nine. Her feet ached in a way that felt earned, almost honorable, and she counted her hours on the bus home: four hours, minimum wage, divided by the cost of the boots she wanted. It was her mother who had insisted she get the job, her father who had made the small speech about responsibility, and it was Maika who had wanted, privately, the money itself, the blunt fact of it, cash that belonged to nobody's judgment but her own.

On Saturday the deli got slammed. Mr. Voss was on the phone with the supplier, and the regular slicer guy had called in, and the line at the case grew six people deep. That was when DeShawn, the seventeen-year-old who had been there eight months and who had trained Maika on the olive scale, pulled his apron strings tighter and stepped behind the slicer.

"DeShawn," Maika said. "You can't."

"It's four pounds of turkey," he said. "They're not going to wait."

"No, I mean legally. You're seventeen. The rules say workers under 18 can't run the power-driven slicer, not in a grocery deli, not in a restaurant, anywhere. Voss told me my first day."

DeShawn's hand stayed on the guard. He looked at her, then at the line, then at Mr. Voss's back. "Eight months I've covered this station."

"Then they've been breaking the rule for eight months." She said it quietly. The woman at the front of the line shifted her weight and checked her phone.

DeShawn stepped back from the machine. He went to the register instead and started taking orders, telling each customer there would be a delay on sliced items, that they could buy the pre-sliced or come back in twenty minutes. One man left. The others stayed. Maika watched DeShawn's face settle into something between anger and relief, and she recognized neither one as her own. She swept the same six tiles she had already swept.

When Mr. Voss hung up the phone, he came over fast. "Who told you to stop slicing?"

"Nobody told me," DeShawn said. "I stopped."

"We've got a line."

"Maika says under-18s can't operate it. Federal rules. She had it on a card."

Mr. Voss looked at Maika. She pulled the laminated card out of her back pocket and held it up, not close enough to be aggressive, just far enough that he had to read it. He read it. His jaw worked once, twice. "Fine," he said finally. "Nobody under 18 touches the slicer. Starting now. Maika, get the pre-sliced from the cooler."

She got it. She restocked the case while DeShawn rang people up and the line shrank, and when the rush ended he came and stood beside her at the sink where she was washing the olive scoops.

"I'm not mad at you," he said. "I'm mad I didn't know. Eight months, and you knew on day one."

"I only knew because he happened to tell me." She handed him a towel. "I didn't figure it out. I just got lucky."

He dried the scoops and stacked them. "Still," he said. "You said no when it counted."

At home she lay on her bed with the laminated card on her stomach, thinking about the difference between knowing a rule and being the person who says it out loud. Her mother had a truism for everything, work hard, keep your head down, and Maika had always assumed the two things fit together, that keeping your head down and doing right were the same act. Tonight they had pulled apart in opposite directions, and she had chosen, and the choice had cost DeShawn nothing and the store a few customers and Mr. Voss some pride, and she could not yet tell whether the whole thing had been brave or merely technical, a girl quoting a card. Maybe by the end of the summer she would know. From the kitchen her mother called that dinner was ready, and Maika put the card in the drawer of her desk, under the bus pass, and went to eat.

story:
Isabelle spread the papers across the kitchen table, smoothing each page flat with the heel of her hand the way her mother did with dough. The phone contract was fourteen pages long, and the line in dispute was on page nine, buried between clauses about roaming charges and something called indemnification. "Unlimited data subject to fair use," it said, and below that, in smaller type, "excess usage may incur charges." Nowhere did it define fair use, or excess, or even what a charge might amount to. The bill sitting beside the contract said eighty-four dollars.

Her mother set down two mugs of tea and pulled out the chair across from her. "What did they say when you called?"

"Nothing useful. The man read the same line back to me twice, like repetition was an argument. He said fair use is whatever their policy says it is."

"That's absurd."

"It's their contract." Isabelle turned the page sideways, as if the ambiguity might fall out at a different angle. "They wrote it. We signed it. Apparently signing means agreeing to things they haven't decided yet."

Her mother sipped her tea and watched her. The kitchen smelled of toast gone slightly too far, and the fridge hummed its one recalcitrant note, the one the repairman had never located. For a moment the older woman considered saying that she had warned her daughter about the free phone, about the whole arrangement being too generous to be innocent, but she held it back. The girl was doing something at the table that looked, from across the steam, like the early stages of a fight worth having. She had seen that posture before, at fourteen, over a grade; at eleven, over a library fine. It always ended the same way, with Isabelle reading everything twice and then going in for the kill. Her mother refilled her own mug and waited.

Isabelle had found the forum at one in the morning, hunched over her laptop with the contract photographed beside her. Someone named TechRescue_77, in a thread four years old, had posted the exact Latin phrase in response to a nearly identical complaint: "Contra proferentem," he had written. "It means an ambiguous term gets read against whoever drafted it. Look it up for your jurisdiction, but it's a common rule." She had looked it up. It was, in fact, common. She had underlined the phrase in her notebook three times, then crossed out two of the underlines because three seemed hysterical.

Now she called the company again, speakerphone on, the contract open between the salt shaker and her untouched toast.

"I understand the bill is disputed," said a new voice, a woman named Dara, region unidentified. "But the account holder agreed to the terms and conditions at activation."

"The terms and conditions are ambiguous," Isabelle said. "Fair use isn't defined anywhere in fourteen pages. I checked twice." She kept her voice level, titrating her own frustration drop by drop, because she had learned from the first call that anger gave them a reason to hang up and patience gave them nowhere to go. "So the ambiguity gets read against the party that drafted it. There's a rule for that. Contra proferentem."

A pause, long enough that the fridge hum became the loudest thing in the room.

"I'd have to escalate that," Dara said.

"Please do."

Isabelle's mother raised her eyebrows over the rim of her mug and said nothing. The bill lay between them like a small indictment, eighty-four dollars of asserted liability for a month of data Isabelle had believed was unlimited, in the ordinary sense of the word, the sense a seventeen-year-old might reasonably hold while streaming lecture recordings for a class she was taking at the community college on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Perhaps the company had meant something narrower. Perhaps, she thought, watching the hold music's tinny melody fill the kitchen, that was exactly the problem: two people could sign the same paper and mean different things by it, and the signature bound them anyway, which made consent a stranger idea than it sounded in the pamphlets.

Dara came back on the line. "We can apply a one-time courtesy credit of sixty dollars to the account."

"Not a courtesy," Isabelle said. "The credit. Because your contract doesn't say what fair use is, and the rule reads that against you."

"We can note the dispute on the account."

"Note it in your own words," Isabelle said. "That's fine. I'll note it in mine too."

She wrote the date in the margin of page nine, next to the smaller type, and underlined it once. Then she tore a piece off the cold toast and ate it anyway, looking at her mother, who slid the jam across the table without a word.
