story:
Clara found her brother in the garage before anyone else arrived, because the garage was where the trumpet lived and Theo treated the trumpet like a person who needed privacy. He was running the same sixteen bars over and over, and even through the half-open door she could tell it was the graduation march, the one that had been dragging behind her all week like a rope tied to her ankle.

"You know nobody actually likes that song," she said. "People like the idea of it. There's a difference."

Theo lowered the trumpet and looked at her the way he looked at slow wifi. "It's not a song, it's a march. Pomp and Circumstance. And it has history, actually." He said this with the smugness of a fifteen-year-old who had spent the afternoon on the internet instead of mowing the lawn. "It became graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905. Edward Elgar was there getting an honorary doctorate of music. So every school that plays it is basically copying Yale."

"Copying Yale. That's the most American thing I've ever heard." Clara sat down on the workbench where their dad kept the antiquated paint cans he refused to throw out, cans labeled with colors the house hadn't been since before she was born. "We're in Ohio, Theo. We've never been to Yale. Nobody at my school has been to Yale."

"Everybody plays it, though. That's the point. It's a tradition."

"A tradition is just a mistake that's old enough to be forgiven," Clara said, and immediately regretted it, because it sounded like something she'd rehearsed, and she had rehearsed it, in the shower, for an argument with her father that hadn't happened yet.

The party started at four. By five the backyard had filled with relatives and classmates and Mr. Petrov from the bakery, and Clara moved through it all in her cotton dress with her diploma somewhere under a stack of cards, accepting congratulations the way you accept change from a cashier, automatically, without counting. Her father kept finding her with food. A plate of wings. A cup of punch. He was trying to allay something, she could tell, some worry he hadn't said out loud, and she let him do it because saying the actual thing out loud was her job, and she kept not doing it.

She had been accepted to a college in Boston with a good financial aid package and a name that made people at parties nod slowly, like a bell being struck. That was the story everyone knew. The other story, the one in the folder under her mattress, was a deferral form, one year, already signed by everyone except her. She wanted the year to work at Petrov's and save money and maybe just breathe, and her father had an adage for that kind of thing, the kind he deployed like a card game move: the early bird, the idle mind, the door that closes. She had counter-adages prepared. She had a whole arsenal. She was afraid that when the moment came, both arsenals would turn out to be made of paper.

The moment came at dusk, near the hors d'oeuvre table, when he said, "So, Boston in August," and handed her a cup of punch she already had.

"I need to tell you something," Clara said, and then heard herself say, "Did you know the march they played today became graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905? Edward Elgar was getting an honorary doctorate of music there. Theo told me."

Her father blinked. "That's what you need to tell me?"

"No." She put the punch down on the table, next to the potato salad, which felt absurd, like setting a glass on a witness stand. "The thing is the deferral. The form's signed except for my line. I want to work this year and go next fall instead."

He was quiet long enough that she could hear Theo, inside, starting the march again, muffled through the screen door, sixteen bars looping like a conversation that kept circling back to its first sentence. She watched her father's face do the arithmetic she'd been dreading, watched the word "Petrov's" land in him somewhere, watched him decide, visibly, not to say any of his adages.

"Okay," he said finally. "Then you'll sign it, and we'll talk about money, and you'll still mow the lawn this summer."

"That's it?"

"You expected the firing squad? You saved a stranger from the firing squad, maybe, but not me." He smiled a small, tired smile that had her grandfather in it. "Your grandmother deferring anything? Impossible. But you, you were always going to do things in your own order. I've had seventeen years to get used to it."

Clara felt the gain and the cost arrive together, the way they apparently did: relief going in, and something like grief going out, grief for the girl in August walking a Boston sidewalk, the one who now would not exist, who had existed in her mind for months and now dissolved. She hugged her father, punch and all, and heard the trumpet stop.

Later, when the party had thinned to the loyalists and the fire pit was going, Theo came out and stood next to her with the trumpet under his arm, smug and sweaty from performing for the cousins. "I dedicate my next piece to the graduate," he announced. "It has history, actually. It became graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905, where Edward Elgar received an honorary doctorate of music."

"You've said that four times today."

"Tradition," Theo said, and raised the trumpet.

"Play something else," she said. "Anything else. Please."

He thought about it, then put the trumpet to his lips anyway, and Clara, who had complained about that march all afternoon, stood there in the firelight and did not move until the last note of it faded over the fence and into the neighbors' yard.

story:
The knife was dull again, and Charlotte had to force it through the onions, which was how people cut themselves, Denise always said, though Denise had been saying it for two years without anyone sharpening anything. Charlotte was sixteen and had the Saturday prep shift, six hours at minimum wage, no overtime because her hours never quite reached forty, a number the schedule seemed to avoid the way her hand avoided the hot flat-top. Taped inside her locker was her AP Bio study sheet, the phylogeny of land plants inked in green, because the walk-in had the best light for memorizing and the cooks didn't mind her muttering about mosses while she portioned chicken.

Renata, the kitchen manager, called her over during the lull. "I'm putting you on sauté next month," she said. "Marcus is leaving." Charlotte felt the sentence land in her chest like something warm. Line cook at sixteen. Her mother had worked restaurants her whole life and never got past the cold station, and here was the door opening early, if she was the kind of employee who deserved it, which meant the kind who didn't make trouble.

After the shift, three of them stayed behind the dumpster where the camera didn't reach: Denise from the salad station, Marco the dishwasher, and Priya who ran the grill. Marco had flyers, and he spoke about the union the way he spoke about everything, flat and doctrinaire, as if there were no honest position besides total commitment and anyone who hesitated was already a collaborator. "Signing cards is how we get the vote," he said. "Then we bargain. Wages, hours, conditions. That's collective bargaining. It's the law they have to come to the table." Charlotte stood with her backpack straps in both hands and said nothing, because a signed card was a name on a list, and lists had a way of being seen.

"Why the first of May, anyway?" Denise asked, rubbing sanitizer smell off her wrists. "My cousin marches every year in Manila and I never knew what for."

"Chicago," Marco said. "The Haymarket affair, May fourth, 1886. It grew out of protests for an eight-hour workday. That's why May first is International Workers' Day in so many countries."

"Eight hours," Denise said, looking back at the kitchen's lit windows, where the closers were still on hour ten.

Charlotte went home and lay on her bed doing the arithmetic she had been avoiding. Her scheduled hours had dropped from thirty-eight to thirty-one the same week she'd asked about overtime for a double she'd covered. Renata had smiled and said the payroll system rounded things differently, and Charlotte had let it go, because she was sixteen and the warm door of the sauté station was worth more than forty dollars. That was the deal she'd made without admitting it was a deal.

The next Saturday, Marco came in with his jaw set like a dropped hinge. "Renata has a card," he said quietly, at the pass. "Somebody's. She's got it in the office." He didn't know whose. Priya thought it was hers; Denise thought it was hers; the walk-in door kept opening and closing and nobody could finish a sentence. Charlotte kept chopping, and the pace of her knife gave nothing away, though her hands knew, before she let her mind know, exactly whose card it was. Three weeks ago, before Renata's promise, before the sauté station, she had signed it in the parking lot with Marco watching and Priya holding the flashlight. She had told herself since then that maybe it didn't count, that she'd been carried along, that a girl who wanted the line had every reason to stay quiet now.

Then the knife slipped on a wet onion and opened the base of her thumb, a clean diagonal welling fast. Denise wrapped it and said it didn't look deep enough for sutures, holding her hand tight above the sink while the blood thinned to pink in the running water. From the office doorway, Renata's voice carried across the kitchen, casual, asking Marco whether he wanted to pick up Sunday, and Charlotte understood that Renata was buying him too, the way she'd bought Charlotte, the way managers bought people in small denominations of hours and promises all the time, and that the card in the office was not an accusation yet but a weight, something Renata could hold until it was useful.

Charlotte dried her hands, walked past the pass, and knocked on the office door frame. Renata looked up from the desk, the card nowhere visible, her face arranged in friendly attention. "I need to put my cut on the incident log," Charlotte said, "and while I'm here, I want to say it's my card. I signed it. If you're going to hold it over anyone, hold it over me." The clock over Renata's shoulder read 9:40. Somewhere behind her the closers were starting hour ten.

Renata closed the log and slid it toward her. "That's a brave thing to say for someone who wants sauté."

Charlotte picked up the pen.

story:
Kayla had counted the keys twice before Mrs. Okafor came back, and both times she got the same impossible answer: eighty-eight. Fifty-two white and thirty-six black, which meant the black keys outnumbered the whites by nothing and were outnumbered by sixteen, a piece of arithmetic she kept rechecking on the corner of her notebook as though the piano might have moved a key when she wasn't looking. The community center's practice room smelled like floor wax and old coffee, and the upright piano against the wall had a chip in the middle C sharp that she had already decided was a scar, not a flaw.

"You're counting again," said Desmond from the doorway. He was the only other Thursday student, seventeen, a saxophonist who treated every waiting room as his personal green room. "You know the piano doesn't change between lessons, right? It's not out here pulling pranks."

"Eighty-eight," Kayla said. "Fifty-two white, thirty-six black. Verify me."

"Verify yourself. I don't do math before six." But he came in and sat on the bench beside her anyway, and his finger hopped along the black keys like a man crossing stepping stones. "Huh. Okay, that's more than I would've guessed. All those little guys add up."

That was the thing she kept chewing on while Mrs. Okafor set up the metronome in the main room, its tick leaking under the door like a heartbeat the building had grown. Kayla had wanted to learn piano for exactly one reason, which she had told nobody: her grandmother had played, back when, and had died in the spring, leaving behind a cassette recording of something fast and bright that nobody in the family could name. Kayla's plan had been simple and, she now suspected, slightly foolish. Learn piano, learn the song, learn the grandmother. She had imagined it as a straight line, like a ladder.

The ladder, it turned out, was eighty-eight rungs wide. Mrs. Okafor had her doing five-finger positions and middle C until Kayla wanted to apologize personally to middle C for all the attention it was receiving. "You want the song," Mrs. Okafor had said last week, not unkindly, "but the song is at the top of the stairs, and you are on the second step, holding the railing, suspicious of the railing." Kayla had gone home and sulked productively, which was her specialty: she would cogitate on a problem until it surrendered or she fell asleep, whichever came first.

Tonight, though, sitting on the bench while the metronome ticked and Desmond hummed something ancillary and annoying behind her, she had a thought that felt less like surrendering and more like switching rivers. If fifty-two white keys and thirty-six black keys could add up to one instrument, then maybe her plan and the actual learning were not opponents. Maybe they were the white and black of the same thing. She didn't have to choose between the boring staircase and the grandmother's ghost of a melody; she had to notice that the staircase was made of the same wood as the song.

"Desmond," she said, "do you ever think about how your saxophone doesn't have a single visible note on it? You press buttons and blow and it just, like, happens."

"That's called skill, Kayla."

"It's called hiding the machinery." She spread her hands across the keys, all the way down, then all the way up, and the reach of it surprised her, shoulders and wrists complaining together. "I can see every note I'm ever going to play. They're all just sitting here waiting. That's either the most encouraging thing I've ever seen or a horror movie."

"A horror movie," Desmond said solemnly. "Definitely a horror movie."

Mrs. Okafor opened the door then, sheet music in hand, and Kayla closed the notebook where the arithmetic lived. She did not say anything about metaphysics or grandmothers or cassette tapes, because she wasn't sure yet whether the whole thought would hold its shape in daylight. What she knew was smaller and sturdier: fifty-two and thirty-six, and her hands resting on all of it.

"Same piece as last week," Mrs. Okafor said, settling into her chair, "but tonight, Kayla, I want you to make one mistake on purpose. Somewhere in the middle. Anywhere. A big, obvious, committed mistake."

"Why would I do that?"

"Because you play like someone standing guard over eighty-eight prisoners, and I want to see what happens when one of them escapes."

Kayla looked at the keys, all lined up and orderly, and started playing.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
story:
The printer at Grandma's house still used the old tray-feed paper, and Madison had to hold each sheet flat while it crawled out, warm and faintly chemical-smelling, like something developing. She had come here for the quiet, three days before the deadline, because at home her little brother debilitated any attempt at concentration by eleven a.m. and her mother treated every open laptop as an invitation to reminisce about her own college years. Here there was only the ticking kitchen clock and Grandma's rule of silence until noon, which Madison had once found oppressive and now found merciful.

The paper was supposed to argue something. Not summarize, her teacher had said, not report; argue. Ten pages, footnotes, a bibliography in Chicago style, which Madison had chosen because the sample page in the handbook looked the most organized, like a filing system for a mind. Her argument was that the federal highway projects of the 1950s had destroyed urban neighborhoods on purpose, not incidentally, and she had found a scholar named Rourke whose book said exactly that, in better sentences than she could write.

That was the problem, actually. Rourke wrote like someone who had walked the demolished streets himself. Madison had typed out one of his paragraphs on the neighborhood in Eastwick, then closed the book and retyped it from memory, changing the words as they came, the way she reworded song lyrics when she didn't want her friends to know what she'd been listening to. Her version was shorter and plainer. It felt like hers now. She moved on to the next section and didn't think about it again, which was either carelessness or a decision; she honestly couldn't have said which.

On the second morning Grandma set down a plate of toast and stood reading over her shoulder, which Madison normally hated. "You're awfully fast with that one book," Grandma said. "In my day we copied things out by hand and called it studying."

"Paraphrasing," Madison said. "It's not copying if you put it in your own words."

Grandma made a small sound, not quite agreement, and went back to the kitchen. Madison stared after her. There was something in the way Grandma had turned away, a haste in it, and it snagged on a memory from years ago: Grandma at the dining room table with her old college friend Helen, the two of them low-voiced over a scrapbook, and Helen saying, "They never proved anything, Ruth, you know that," and Grandma saying, "Everyone knew," and then silence when they noticed Madison in the doorway. Madison had been eight. She had thought they were talking about a man.

The clock ticked. Madison pulled the handbook back toward her and looked up plagiarism in the index, mostly to prove Grandma wrong, and the page said it plainly: plagiarism covers using ideas without credit, not only copying exact wording. Putting another writer's idea into your own words still requires a citation. She read it twice, then three times, the way you reread a sentence that has quietly rearranged the furniture of a room. Her Eastwick paragraph sat on the screen, plain and hers and not hers.

She went into the kitchen. Grandma was wiping a counter that was already clean, which she did when she wanted to seem occupied. "Did you ever get in trouble?" Madison asked. "At school. For something you wrote."

The cloth stopped. Grandma looked at the window above the sink, where the maple had gone yellow and was letting go of itself a leaf at a time, melancholic and unhurried, and Madison understood that her grandmother was deciding how much of the past was an encumbrance worth carrying into the light. "Helen and I wrote for the same magazine in sixty-one," Grandma said. "I used her research. Her idea about the textile mills. I didn't copy a word of it. I thought that made it mine." She folded the cloth into a perfect square. "She stopped speaking to me for two years. Longer, really. It was never the same after."

"I have to go fix something," Madison said, and her voice came out strange.

She went back and reread Rourke's paragraph against her own, side by side, and saw that she had kept his structure, his sequence of facts, his conclusion, and changed only the surface, like repainting a borrowed car. She typed a footnote number after the Eastwick paragraph, then sat with the cursor blinking in the footnote field, because the citation format wanted a page number and she had to go find it, which meant admitting, in the physical act of turning pages, what she had done. She turned the pages. Page 214. She wrote it down.

At lunch Grandma brought sandwiches without being asked and set one beside the laptop. "Fixed?" she said.

"Footnote four," Madison said, and pointed at the screen. Grandma leaned over, read it slowly, her lips moving a little, and then she straightened up and squeezed Madison's shoulder once, hard, the way she did when words would have been worse.

"Make it five while you're at it," she said. "I saw another one."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
story:
Nevaeh adjusted the mirror before her mother could tell her to, and the car seemed to settle around her, its smallness suddenly apparent, the roof close enough to touch. The parking lot of the community college was empty on a Saturday morning except for a groundskeeper pushing a cart along the far fence. She turned the key the way the manual had said, and the engine caught on the first try, which felt like a small mercy.

"Foot on the brake before you shift," her mother said, but Nevaeh had already done it, having read the chapter twice the night before, once at the kitchen table and once in bed with the flashlight her little brother used for reading comics under his blanket. She eased the car into drive. The lot's painted lines slid past the windshield, white and patient.

Her brother Marcus had gotten his permit two months before her, on the day he turned sixteen, and had spent that evening mapping out all the places he would take people. Lake behind the middle school, the taco truck on Fourth, his friend Dario's house out past the golf course. He had gone around the kitchen reciting names like a man distributing gifts. Then their mother had told him the sequence, and Nevaeh, thirteen then, had watched his face reorganize itself.

"It's called graduated licensing," Marcus had said that night, flat with disappointment, turning the laminated permit over in his hands. "First the permit, then a provisional license with restrictions, and only after that the full license." He had read it off the state website himself, slowly, as though saying it aloud might make it negotiable. It did not. He had sat in the driveway the next day anyway, in the driver's seat of the empty car, not driving anywhere, just holding the wheel with both hands.

In the lot, her mother said, "Signal, then check your mirror, then look over your shoulder. The signal doesn't replace the look." Nevaeh signaled, checked, looked. The empty lot offered no consequence for carelessness, which was somehow its own problem; she wanted the stakes to be real so that her attention would be real too. She pulled out onto the access road, and the first oncoming car passed close enough that she gripped the wheel tighter than she meant to.

"You're fine," her mother said. "He had the whole other lane."

They drove the loop around the college, past the gymnasium and the bus turn-around, and Nevaeh began to feel the pedal under her foot as a conversation rather than a command. Press, ease, press. When a bicyclist appeared ahead on the shoulder, she slowed early, well before she needed to, wanting to forestall any possibility of the woman on the bike having to make a decision about her. Her mother noticed. "That was good. Early is better than late."

At the stop sign at the edge of campus, Nevaeh braked fully and sat for a second with her hands at ten and two. "Can I ask you something?" she said.

"You just did."

"Mom."

"Ask."

"Do you think the rules are right? The ones Marcus hates. That you can't just get your license and drive whoever you want." She watched a sparrow cross in front of the hood and land on the sign itself, unbothered by the machinery idling below it.

Her mother was quiet long enough that Nevaeh thought she was composing something sagacious, the kind of thing adults kept in a drawer for occasions like this. Instead she said, "When I was seventeen I failed my first road test. Rolled a stop sign. My father said the examiner was too strict. I knew he was right and my father was being kind." She tapped the window with one finger. "I needed someone to not be kind about that particular thing."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the material for one. Go when you're ready."

Nevaeh went, turning left onto the busier road, and the traffic made everything she did meaningful. She held her speed. She thought about Marcus in the driveway, and about the bicyclist, and about the rolled stop sign from twenty years ago, and she understood that she was being asked to hold two things at once: that the restrictions were a shape imposed on her from outside, and that the shape was drawn around a real danger that she, personally, statistically, embodied. Sixteen-year-olds were not a phenotype you could select against, but they were, as a group, the thing the rule was drawn around. She was inside the group whether she drove well or badly, and the rule did not know her, and the rule might still be right. Both of those could be true. She wasn't sure yet how to live inside a rule that didn't know her, whether that was humility or erasure, and she decided she would have to keep driving long enough to find out.

"Turn here," her mother said, "and pull over where the curb is flat."

Nevaeh signaled, checked, looked over her shoulder, and brought the car to the curb in one smooth arc that surprised her with its competence. She set the brake and let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding.

"So can I drive us home?" she said.

"Permit," her mother said, and unclipped her seatbelt to slide over. "You drive, I ride, and neither of us tells Marcus you did better than him on day one."

"He already knows he was worse," Nevaeh said, and then, as she pulled back onto the road, "I'll drive him to the taco truck when I'm allowed. First thing."

Her mother was already halfway out the door and laughing. "Get your seatbelt," she said, "before I change my mind about everything."

story:
Mr. Kwan hired me on a Tuesday, and by Friday I had already decided he was stealing from me. I want to be clear about that up front, because I was wrong, and because being wrong took me three days and a woman named Delores to figure out. I am good at math. I tutor freshmen in algebra for gas money. So when my first envelope came up short, I did the only reasonable thing: I multiplied my hours by my rate, checked it twice, and stared at the difference like it was a stranger standing in my kitchen.

The job itself was fine. Holsom's Hardware, two aisles of paint and a back wall of screws sorted into little drawers nobody had alphabetized since the nineties. Mr. Kwan wanted me Saturdays and two afternoons a week, restocking, running the register when the line got long. I'd applied because the transmission in my mother's Corolla was making a sound like a spoon in a garbage disposal, and the shop in Bellview wanted five hundred dollars by the following Friday or they'd release the bay to someone else. That was my deadline, and I was watching it the way you watch a pot you're sure is about to boil over.

The envelope said I'd worked nineteen hours at nine dollars an hour. That was one hundred seventy-one dollars. The check inside was for one hundred sixty point four zero. I did it on the register's scrap paper during my break, then again at home on the good calculator. Ten dollars and sixty cents, gone. I told myself it was an accounting error, but somewhere between Holsom's and my bedroom the idea began to calcify into something harder: Mr. Kwan had quietly shaved the number, assuming a sixteen-year-old wouldn't notice. That's what people assume about us. That we can't multiply.

Saturday I tested him. I asked, casually, whether the register printed hours wrong sometimes. He said the register was fine. I asked whether pay ever got "adjusted" for new employees, and he looked at me over his glasses and said no, and I thought, well, he would say that. My mother's mechanic called that afternoon to say the price had gone up to five forty. I hung up and lay on my bed doing the arithmetic of my life: five hundred forty dollars, minus one hundred sixty point four zero, minus the eighty in my sock drawer, meant I needed three more paychecks, which meant the Corolla sat dead in the driveway for weeks. Something had to be wrong with the math. Somebody's math.

Delores worked the register on Sundays, a big slow-moving woman who had been at Holsom's for eleven years and referred to every customer under thirty as a detractor of the human race, though she said it with something close to affection. I came in on my day off, ostensibly to buy masking tape, actually to ask her whether Mr. Kwan had ever shorted her. She laughed so hard she had to grip the counter.

"Boy, sit down," she said, and pulled a stool over. "You did your hours times your rate." I said yes. "And it came up short by about six percent." I admitted it was six and a fifth percent, precisely, because I had computed it to the second decimal, and she laughed again. "That's Social Security," she said. "Employers withhold six point two percent of your wages for Social Security tax, up to a yearly wage limit." She said it flat, like reading a label. "Mine stops coming out around August. I make enough by then that I hit the limit. Yours won't stop. You won't get near it."

I sat there recalculating in my head, and the whole edifice of my suspicion came apart in about four seconds. Six point two percent of one hundred seventy-one is ten point six zero two. Mr. Kwan hadn't taken anything. The number was the number. Delores watched me do it, watched my face change, and said nothing, which I've since decided was the kindest thing anyone did for me that month.

What stays uncertain is this: I still don't know exactly what I was so ready to believe about him, or why the missing ten dollars felt like proof of something larger, some story I'd already written about adults and shortcuts. I apologized Monday, mumbled something about my math being off, and he shrugged and handed me a box of washers to sort. I didn't tell my mother any of it. I called the shop in Bellview, asked about a payment plan, and then, while I was waiting on hold, started sorting the washers by size, smallest first, my fingers moving faster than my thoughts for once.

Delores came through the back door with her coffee and looked at the row of little drawers I'd lined up across the counter. "Look at that," she said. "The profligate one, organizing."

"Mr. Kwan's nephew," I said. "He's the profligate one. He ordered three kinds of washers nobody buys."

She sat down on her stool and pointed at the smallest drawer. "Start there. Tell me which ones we actually sell."

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
story:
Jasmine had acclimated to the smell of the bakery by her third shift, which was faster than most new hires managed, according to Dev at the cash register. Her job was simple on paper: box the pastries, work the till on weekends, count the drawer at close. The till was the part that taught her things. Every sale rang up two extra lines, five percent federal and seven percent provincial, added on top of the sticker price, and every so often a customer would stare at their receipt like it had lied to them.

She was counting out change on a Saturday afternoon when Priya texted her a photo. Priya was in Manchester for the summer, staying with her aunt, and the photo was of a receipt from a coffee shop. "Why does nothing add up here," the message read. "Muffin says £2.40 on the shelf, receipt says £2.40. Where's the tax?"

Jasmine leaned against the counter between customers and looked at her own receipt tape, the one still curling out of the register. Her £2.40 equivalent, a three-dollar croissant, rang up as $3.36. She typed back that taxes got added at the till in Canada, on top of the price. Priya sent a shrug emoji, then a screenshot of a UK government page. Jasmine read it twice. The United Kingdom's standard rate of VAT, a sales tax built into most prices, had been 20 percent since January 4, 2011.

"So the tax is hiding inside the price," Jasmine said out loud, mostly to herself.

"They call it VAT," Priya wrote. "Value added tax." That was all the message said, and somehow that made it clearer than a paragraph would have.

Dev looked over from the bread slicer. "Talking to your British girlfriend?" He said it the way he said everything, flat, and Jasmine didn't bother correcting him. She was doing arithmetic in her head, dividing £2.40 by 1.2, getting £2.00, watching forty pence of tax dissolve into a shelf price. It felt almost like arbitrage, knowing the true cost of a thing while everyone else paid the polite number on the tag, though she knew that wasn't what arbitrage meant. It was closer to being let in on a quiet arrangement.

Friday was payday. Jasmine had been waiting for the cheque all month because she needed ninety dollars for the deposit on a used amp, and her first full pay period, with two weeks of closing shifts folded in, should have cleared it easily. She opened the envelope in the back room and stood very still. The number was smaller than she'd worked out in her notebook, smaller by about forty dollars, and under the gross pay line were deductions she hadn't fully accounted for: income tax, and something called CPP, and EI. She'd known they existed the way you know weather exists, as a general condition. She hadn't thought they'd arrive so soon, in her first month, at seventeen.

She brought the stub to Dev, who squinted at it. "You filled out your TD1?" She didn't know what that was. He shrugged. "Ask payroll. Or claim it back, you make nothing, you'll get a refund when you file." She wrote the numbers on the back of the receipt from the amp seller, who'd held it for her until Monday, and she felt the small tectonic shift of a plan grinding against a fact. Ninety dollars minus the shortfall. She counted the bills in her wallet twice, as if arithmetic might renegotiate.

That night her mother found her at the kitchen table with the stub, the UK receipt photo, and her own receipt from the bakery laid side by side. "What's all this?" her mother asked, and Jasmine explained: here a tax you can see being added, there a tax folded into the price so quietly you had to do division to find it, and on her paycheque a tax taken before the money ever reached her, which was somehow the quietest of all. "Different systems," her mother said, filling the kettle. "All of them take their share. You just learn where to look."

On Monday Jasmine went to the amp seller's basement door with fifty-five dollars and the rest promised from the next pay period, and while the man considered it she checked his handwritten receipt and saw he'd charged no tax at all. "You're supposed to charge HST," she said, not sure why she said it, and he looked at her a long moment before reaching for the cord.

"Take it," he said. "Fifty-five, and we forget the paperwork."

She carried the amp up the stairs and out into the street, and only at the corner did she realize she'd left all three receipts on her mother's table, the evidence of everything she'd worked out, and she turned back toward the house instead of the bus stop.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
story:
Levi had worked the front desk at Ridgeview Fitness for five weeks, long enough to learn the register, the towel count, and the laminated script for new members. The script was taped to the underside of the counter, and it used words he had never said out loud before his first shift: terms, conditions, liability waiver, monthly billing authorization. He said them forty times a week now. They had sensitized him to the paperwork everywhere else, too. He read his phone plan's renewal notice twice on the bus home, looking for the trap.

On a Tuesday evening in August, a boy came in with a duffel bag and a folded printout of the membership offer. His name was Marcus, he was seventeen, and he wanted the student rate before football conditioning started. He had a debit card in his hand and a school ID. Levi slid the contract across the counter and handed him the pen, and Marcus signed his name in careful block letters, and everything would have been fine except the form asked for his date of birth, and Marcus wrote it honestly.

"I need a parent's signature," Levi said. "It's the policy."

"Both my parents work nights," Marcus said. "I have the money. I have the card. What does it matter whose name is on the line?"

Levi did not have an answer. He looked at the script under the counter, but the script only covered pricing tiers and cancellation fees. He told Marcus he would ask his manager and hold the paperwork in the drawer, and Marcus said he would come back Thursday, and he took the pen with him by accident, a small theft neither of them noticed.

The manager, Ms. Okafor, was off until morning. Levi's coworker Danny was on the closing shift, and Danny was a dilettante who had opinions on contract law, real estate, sourdough starters, and the zoning dispute at the taco place across the street. "It's because he could cancel it," Danny said, spraying the treadmills. "A minor signs, a minor can walk away from it. That's the whole thing. It's voidable by the minor. Look it up if you don't believe me."

"I'm not looking up your theories."

"Look up whoever you want. It's common law, it's most of the country. The gym can't hold a kid to a contract. Kid can void it, gym can't. That's why they want the parent." Danny pointed the spray bottle at him. "There are exceptions. Necessities. Food, that kind of thing. A gym membership is not a necessity, no matter what Marcus's football coach thinks."

Levi did look it up, on his break, sitting on the stacked mats in the stretching corner with his phone. Danny had it right, which annoyed him. In common-law jurisdictions, including most of the US, a contract made by a minor was generally voidable by the minor, with exceptions such as contracts for necessities. Levi read the sentence three times. It was not that Marcus could not sign. It was that his signature meant one thing for the gym and another thing for Marcus, and the gym had decided it did not like the arrangement.

The next morning Levi found the policy binder behind the desk, and in the membership section there was a memo in Ms. Okafor's florid handwriting, all loops and crossed sevens, dated three years back: No memberships to under-18s without parent or guardian signature. Refund if already billed. Levi read it and understood that the policy was not a rule about who could join. It was a rule about risk. The gym wanted a signature it could enforce, and Marcus's parents, working nights, were the enforceable ones.

When Ms. Okafor came in at ten, Levi asked her about it. "What if the parent can't come in? Can they mail it, or do it over the phone?"

"They can mail it, they can fax it if they find a fax machine, they can come in on a Sunday," she said. "Why, do you have one?"

"Kid came in last night. Football season. He's coming back Thursday."

"Then Thursday we get him the form to take home." She was restocking the protein bars and did not look up. "Or he waits until his birthday."

Levi spent Wednesday thinking about it during the slow hours, between checking people in and wiping down the key rack. He had assumed the policy was a wall. Now it looked more like a door with a particular handle, and the question was whether he was supposed to tell Marcus where the handle was. He could explain the whole thing: that Marcus's own signature was legal but fragile, voidable, that the gym wanted his parents because their signatures could not be taken back. He could also just say "policy" again, the way the script did, and let Marcus believe there was nothing on the other side.

Thursday evening Marcus came back, duffel over his shoulder, and put the stolen pen on the counter without comment. "My dad's asleep by the time I get home," he said. "He sleeps at four in the afternoon. Conditioning starts Monday. If I'm not there Monday, they give my spot to a junior."

Levi took the contract out of the drawer and laid it flat. He turned it so Marcus could read it, and put his finger under the line that said the agreement was voidable by any member under eighteen, that exceptions applied only to contracts for necessities. "That's why they need your dad," he said. "Not because you can't sign. Because you can sign and then cancel it whenever you want, and they can't stop you, and they hate that. Your dad's signature they can hold onto."

Marcus read the paragraph twice. "So if I sign it and they bill me, I can void it?"

"That's what it says. I looked it up. It's most of the country, the common-law places. I'm not a lawyer."

"And a gym isn't a necessity."

"That's the exception, apparently. Food, stuff like that. Not this." Levi slid the take-home form across the counter, the one with the second signature line, and set the pen on top of it.
